scoreNote: Strong (5): a policy-appropriate response that weighs the consequences of institutional dissuasion, shows why they are harmful, and answers the legitimate concern with a better alternative; well organized and persuasive.

sentences.text: A university naturally wants its students to succeed, and it can feel kind to steer the likely failures away before they waste their years and their money.
From this impulse comes the proposed policy: that educational institutions should actively dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.

However well meant, I believe this policy would do far more harm than good, because predictions of failure are notoriously unreliable and the act of dissuasion would crush the very ambition that schools exist to nurture.

sections.role: Body — Predictions of failure are unreliable

sentences.text: First, implementing the policy would require institutions to predict who will fail, and such predictions are far less accurate than they look.
Talent often reveals itself slowly, and a field that seems the wrong fit at eighteen can become a life's calling by twenty-two.
Late bloomers, students who stumbled early and flourished later, and those who simply needed a different teacher fill the history of every discipline.
Einstein was an unremarkable student, and countless accomplished professionals once looked hopeless in the very field they came to master.
Many disciplines reward persistence as much as raw aptitude, and persistence is exactly what an early prediction cannot measure.
A policy that acted on early signs of weakness would inevitably turn away many who would have succeeded, a cost no institution should impose so casually.
Worse, judgments about who is unlikely to succeed are easily distorted by prejudice.
Throughout history women were told they could not do science and the poor were told they did not belong at university, predictions that reflected bias rather than ability.
A policy of dissuasion would hand institutions a respectable-sounding excuse to push disadvantaged students out of demanding fields, hardening the very inequalities education should dissolve.
The phrase unlikely to succeed attaches most easily to exactly the students who have always been told they do not belong.
A confident prediction of failure can also become self-fulfilling, draining the very motivation a student needs to prove it wrong.
The consequence would be a narrower, less diverse, and less just set of professions.
The policy does respond to a genuine problem, and that much should be granted.
Students who pour years and savings into a field for which they are truly unsuited suffer real and avoidable harm.
But the answer is to inform, not to dissuade: institutions should offer honest feedback, clear data about outcomes, and frank guidance, then let students choose.
Such counsel respects students as adults capable of weighing risk, whereas dissuasion treats a fallible prediction as a verdict and quietly closes a door that was theirs to open.
Treated as capable adults, students tend to rise to the responsibility; treated as likely failures, many simply give up.
The distance between advising and dissuading is the distance between empowering a choice and overriding it.
In conclusion, the consequences of a policy of dissuasion would clearly outweigh its benefits.
Because predictions fail, because bias creeps in, and because ambition matters, institutions should equip students to make wise choices rather than make those choices for them.
Education should widen the range of what a young person might become, not quietly shrink it.
A school's task is to open doors and tell the truth about what lies beyond them, not to bar the doors it doubts a student can walk through.
